speaker: The Announcer
text: On this season of LAiDIES: she stops feeling behind.

speaker: The Announcer
text: She learns to delegate to machines — without lowering her standards.

speaker: The Announcer
text: She builds her own little squad of AI helpers.

speaker: The Announcer
text: And she becomes the woman other people come to when the future gets confusing.

speaker: The Announcer
text: And on this episode: our heroine finally stops putting it off.

speaker: The Announcer
text: This is Episode One: On Wednesdays We Do AI.

speaker: The Heroine
text: It's 4:52 on a Tuesday afternoon, and a man named Steve is being called a visionary.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Steve works in revenue operations.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Steve has never once refilled the printer.

speaker: The Heroine
text: And Steve has just presented a competitive analysis — clean, confident, suspiciously well-formatted — that everyone in that room knows took him about an hour, because at lunch he was playing pickleball.

speaker: The Heroine
text: I know because he told us.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Twice.

speaker: The Heroine
text: And me?

speaker: The Heroine
text: I had a version of that same analysis.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Mine took two weekends.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Mine had footnotes.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Mine was still sitting in my drafts folder, waiting until it felt... ready.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Somewhere between Steve's standing ovation and my fourth coffee, it hit me.

speaker: The Heroine
text: He isn't smarter than me.

speaker: The Heroine
text: He isn't better informed.

speaker: The Heroine
text: He just stopped doing it the hard way.

speaker: The Heroine
text: And I couldn't help but wonder... when did everyone learn to do that?

speaker: The Heroine
text: And when, exactly, was I supposed to?

speaker: The Heroine
text: Welcome to LAiDIES — where smart, busy women learn AI one Wednesday at a time, from a little internet town called SUNNYVAiLE.

speaker: The Heroine
text: New here? check out the trailer first.

speaker: The Heroine
text: It's the tour.

speaker: The Heroine
text: This is where the story starts.

speaker: The Heroine
text: And that "she" from the promo?

speaker: The Heroine
text: That's me.

speaker: The Heroine
text: I'm telling this from a few steps ahead — I've made the mistakes, done the reading, and kept the receipts — and as the season goes on, you'll hear from other women figuring it out in real time.

speaker: The Heroine
text: This isn't a lecture.

speaker: The Heroine
text: It's a group chat.

speaker: The Heroine
text: So if Steve sounded familiar — if you have ever sat on work that was better than what got the applause — get in loser.

speaker: The Heroine
text: We're learning AI...

speaker: The Heroine
text: So.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Let me tell you what I did after the Steve meeting.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Nothing.

speaker: The Heroine
text: For six months.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Well — not nothing.

speaker: The Heroine
text: I did what every competent woman does with a problem she doesn't have time for: I put it on a list.

speaker: The Heroine
text: And in my defense, every time I tried to start, the on-ramp was terrible.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Everything I found was either written by men in fleece vests — say no more — or so surface-level it basically amounted to "AI is transformative!" AI is transformative?

speaker: The Heroine
text: Groundbreaking.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Here's the thing.

speaker: The Heroine
text: I have a full-time job.

speaker: The Heroine
text: I manage a team.

speaker: The Heroine
text: My calendar is a Tetris game I am perpetually losing.

speaker: The Heroine
text: So the idea of adding "become AI-literate" to that pile felt about as realistic as Miranda Priestly asking me to fetch the unpublished Harry Potter manuscript.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Technically possible — but at what personal cost?

speaker: The Heroine
text: Then one night — eleven p.m., everyone else asleep, glass of wine — I went looking for a different answer.

speaker: The Heroine
text: And somewhere past the third search result...

speaker: The Heroine
text: I found a town.

speaker: The Heroine
text: An actual little internet town, permanently set in nineteen ninety-nine, with a main street, a radio station, and a library that never closes.

speaker: The Heroine
text: It's that kind of place.

speaker: The Heroine
text: I didn't know it yet, but I was moving in.

speaker: The Heroine
text: And that first night, in that library, the question I brought wasn't "how do I learn AI." It was: is it just me?

speaker: The Heroine
text: It was not just me.

speaker: The Heroine
text: I found a Harvard study.

speaker: The Heroine
text: A hundred and forty thousand people, around the world.

speaker: The Heroine
text: For every one hundred men using generative AI tools... seventy-eight women.

speaker: The Heroine
text: And that gap holds even when you control for job type, age, education, and access.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Same tools.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Same desks.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Different adoption rates.

speaker: The Heroine
text: And the deeper I read, the worse it got.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Men are twenty-three percent more likely to be encouraged by their managers to use AI.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Twenty-seven percent more likely to be praised when they do.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Steve got called a visionary, remember.

speaker: The Heroine
text: And women?

speaker: The Heroine
text: We're thirty-two percent more likely to worry that using AI looks like cutting corners.

speaker: The Heroine
text: That one hit me like Samantha Jones delivering an uncomfortable truth over brunch.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Because of course we worry about that.

speaker: The Heroine
text: We've spent entire careers building credibility through preparation, thoroughness, visible effort.

speaker: The Heroine
text: And now there's a tool that makes hard things look easy — and some part of our brain calculates, correctly, based on historical data, that "easy" might get held against us.

speaker: The Heroine
text: That's not imposter syndrome.

speaker: The Heroine
text: That's pattern recognition.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Which is ironic, given what AI actually is — but we'll get there.

speaker: The Heroine
text: You know how there's always one person who preps the deck before the meeting, remembers the feedback from last time, follows up on the action items nobody else tracked — and still delivers her own work on time?

speaker: The Heroine
text: That person is usually not named Steve.

speaker: The Heroine
text: No offense to the Steves out there fighting the good fight.

speaker: The Heroine
text: So no — this was never a confidence problem.

speaker: The Heroine
text: It's a physics problem.

speaker: The Heroine
text: You cannot add hours to a day that's already over-subscribed.

speaker: The Heroine
text: And the irony is, the tool that could give you your time back requires time you don't have to learn it.

speaker: The Heroine
text: So you don't start.

speaker: The Heroine
text: And the gap compounds, week over week, until the distance between you and the colleague who started six months ago isn't a gap anymore.

speaker: The Heroine
text: It's a canyon.

speaker: The Heroine
text: As Dolly would say...

speaker: The Heroine
text: You'd better get to building your own bridge, honey — because ain't nobody building it for you.

speaker: The Heroine
text: One more thing I found that night, from Fei-Fei Li — the Stanford professor they call the Godmother of AI.

speaker: The Heroine
text: She said it plainly:

speaker: The Heroine
text: If we don't get women involved in AI, we're going to have a future built by half the population — for all of the population.

speaker: The Heroine
text: And it's not just the principle of the thing.

speaker: The Heroine
text: When women don't use these tools, the tools learn from a skewed pool of users — they literally get worse for women.

speaker: The Heroine
text: And around the cycle goes.

speaker: The Heroine
text: So this was never just about my career, or yours.

speaker: The Heroine
text: So here's what finally got me to start.

speaker: The Heroine
text: It wasn't inspiration.

speaker: The Heroine
text: It was spite.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Fine — it was mostly spite, plus a Sunday morning at the Blend and Snap — my corner table, an oat latte going cold, the radio on low — fifteen quiet minutes, and nothing to lose.

speaker: The Heroine
text: There was an email I'd been avoiding for four days.

speaker: The Heroine
text: You know the kind — the delicate one, to the stakeholder who reads tone into line breaks.

speaker: The Heroine
text: I opened one of the AI tools, and instead of asking it something grand, I just told it the truth: who the email was for, what I needed from them, and what I couldn't say out loud.

speaker: The Heroine
text: It gave me a draft in nine seconds.

speaker: The Heroine
text: And it was... eighty percent right.

speaker: The Heroine
text: The other twenty percent was wrong in ways only I could see — which, it turns out, is the good news.

speaker: The Heroine
text: I fixed it with my own judgment.

speaker: The Heroine
text: I hit send.

speaker: The Heroine
text: And then I looked at the clock.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Four days of dread.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Eleven minutes of work.

speaker: The Heroine
text: And that's when it landed: oh.

speaker: The Heroine
text: I can do this.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Because the thing stopping me was never ability.

speaker: The Heroine
text: It was that nobody had explained it in a way that made me want to start.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Now — I want to be clear.

speaker: The Heroine
text: I am no AI slayer.

speaker: The Heroine
text: There's no Watcher guiding me through some prophecy, no training montage that happened off-screen.

speaker: The Heroine
text: I'm still learning, still getting things wrong, still googling things mid-conversation.

speaker: The Heroine
text: But here's my favourite stat I've found so far, and it's the one that keeps me going.

speaker: The Heroine
text: BCG looked at senior women in tech — the ones who push through that first awkward phase.

speaker: The Heroine
text: And they're not trailing the men.

speaker: The Heroine
text: They're out in front — already using these tools more than their male peers, by fourteen percentage points.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Fourteen.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Not because they had some head start — but because they were more aware it mattered, and more willing to take the leap.

speaker: The Heroine
text: You don't claw your way to senior without learning to bet on yourself.

speaker: The Heroine
text: And what they bring to it is the one thing AI cannot replicate: a career's worth of professional judgment.

speaker: The Heroine
text: The instinct that something is off in a document before you can even articulate why.

speaker: The Heroine
text: That twenty percent of my email only I could see?

speaker: The Heroine
text: That's your critical thinking.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Which brings me to my favourite part of every episode.

speaker: The Heroine
text: We call it the cocktail party explanation, and it was born at the Bronze Age — that's our bar in SUNNYVAiLE — during businesswomen's special happy hour.

speaker: The Heroine
text: I was three sips into telling my girlfriends about the email thing when one of them put down her drink and said, "okay, but what IS it?

speaker: The Heroine
text: Actually?" The table went quiet.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Everybody wanted to know.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Nobody wanted to be the one to ask.

speaker: The Heroine
text: So now, every week, this segment hands you the answer you'll give the next time somebody at a dinner table — or a happy hour — says "AI" like they know what they're talking about.

speaker: The Heroine
text: This week's question is the big one: what is this thing, actually?

speaker: The Heroine
text: And I'll give you exactly what I gave the girls.

speaker: The Heroine
text: It's the most talented new hire you'll ever manage.

speaker: The Heroine
text: That's it.

speaker: The Heroine
text: It fits in the lull before the drinks arrive, and it holds up under every follow-up — so let me show you why.

speaker: The Heroine
text: A brilliant new hire has read everything: books, articles, forums, manuals, billions of documents — it's absorbed how language works, how ideas connect, how arguments get built.

speaker: The Heroine
text: That's why it sounds so impressive.

speaker: The Heroine
text: And it has lived nothing: no job, no relationships, no consequences, not one awkward moment at a holiday party that taught it something about people.

speaker: The Heroine
text: So the honest picture isn't a robot genius, and it isn't a toy.

speaker: The Heroine
text: It's day-one talent: superhuman range, astonishing speed, first drafts that'll genuinely scare you — and no read on your office politics, no stake in what happens if it's wrong.

speaker: The Heroine
text: That's where you come in.

speaker: The Heroine
text: You don't hand it the keys — you onboard it.

speaker: The Heroine
text: You give it guidance and guardrails, the lay of the land around the office.

speaker: The Heroine
text: You manage it, and you review its work.

speaker: The Heroine
text: And you've done this all before.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Now — under the hood, when you type something into ChatGPT, or Claude, or Gemini, what it's doing is prediction — generating what comes next, word by word.

speaker: The Heroine
text: And here's the strange part: it's still just that, underneath.

speaker: The Heroine
text: But what grew out of all that prediction — it drafts, it reasons, it'll even run multi-step errands for you — is impressive enough that the experts genuinely can't agree on what to call it, or even whether "reasoning" is the right word.

speaker: The Heroine
text: We'll get to all of that later in the season.

speaker: The Heroine
text: But two limits are not up for debate (and yes, in this case the limits DO exist) — and they're the two that decide whether it helps you or embarrasses you.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Limit one: it does not know your context until you hand it over.

speaker: The Heroine
text: It's Cher's closet computer from Clueless: endless outfit combinations, all day long — but it has no idea the meeting is with a conservative client who is already looking for reasons to dismiss you... unless you tell it.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Remember my email?

speaker: The Heroine
text: I told it the truth about who it was for, and it used every word of that.

speaker: The Heroine
text: The context lives with you.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Handing it over well — that's a skill, and it's literally next week's episode.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Limit two: out of the box, it does not check whether what it says is true.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Only whether it's plausible.

speaker: The Heroine
text: It's the Burn Book from Mean Girls: some entries accurate, some completely fabricated, all delivered with the same unbothered confidence.

speaker: The Heroine
text: "Made out with a hot dog"?

speaker: The Heroine
text: Same certainty as an actual fact — it has no way of telling the two apart.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Regina George energy.

speaker: The Heroine
text: But make it AI.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Three words before you go, so you don't pull a Cher, confidently arguing it doesn't say R.S.V.P. on the Statue of Liberty.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Generative AI: the kind that makes new things — text, images, first drafts.

speaker: The Heroine
text: A Carrie Bradshaw in your laptop — not one that finds you articles to read, that's Google — one that writes the column for you.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Model: the trained brain behind the app.

speaker: The Heroine
text: ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini are the magazines; the models are their editors-in-chief — different taste, different judgment, different style.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Same brief, wildly different results.

speaker: The Heroine
text: And hallucination: when the answer comes back polished, confident... and partly or completely made up.

speaker: The Heroine
text: It's not lying — lying takes intent.

speaker: The Heroine
text: It's guessing.

speaker: The Heroine
text: The newer models are better at it — they'll flag when they're unsure, and if you hand them a source, they'll actually check it.

speaker: The Heroine
text: But better isn't fixed: push one past what it really knows and it'll still answer with total authority.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Think of your most confident friend, who'll answer any question whether or not she really knows.

speaker: The Heroine
text: I'm not a regular mom — I'm a cool mom.

speaker: The Heroine
text: That's AI trying to be helpful and completely misreading the room.

speaker: The Heroine
text: And your job, in all of this, is knowing which parts to trust and which to push back on.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Which — good news — is exactly what you've been doing with other people's work your entire career, and we're going to help you apply those skills to AI over the season.

speaker: The Heroine
text: And... that's the episode.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Now — your try-on.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Not homework; this isn't school.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Ten minutes, and everything you need lives at laidies.ai.

speaker: The Heroine
text: That's "LAiDIES" spelled with an i in the middle: L, A, i, D, I, E, S.

speaker: The Heroine
text: And if you'd rather read than listen, the whole episode's written up there too — every stat and study laid out where you can find it again.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Inside is the try-on, and this week, you're holding auditions: open the three big tools — ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini — and give all three the same small, real task.

speaker: The Heroine
text: My avoided email, or your version of it.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Tell them the truth about who it's for and what you need, then compare the three drafts that come back.

speaker: The Heroine
text: They won't match (that's the editors-in-chief thing).

speaker: The Heroine
text: One of them will win today's task.

speaker: The Heroine
text: A different one might win next week's, because the tools are genuinely good at different things — and learning which one to reach for, for what, is part of the fluency we're building.

speaker: The Heroine
text: And in every draft, notice the twenty percent only you can see.Then, if you're feeling it: take the pop quiz at SUNNYVAiLE High — ten questions on today's episode, plus 2 bonus questions your score banks butterfly clips, and yes, that will make sense when you get there.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Turn on K-S-V-L, ninety-nine point nine, for this week's anthem — don't just learn from books, learn from hooks.

speaker: The Heroine
text: And if you've got time to wander, the town is full of extras: get your cards read at Madame Cleo's, call nineteen ninety-nine from the Dream Phone, ask the Fairy Godmother anything — and somewhere around town there's hidden charms.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Find one, and it's yours.

speaker: The Heroine
text: And if this is your first Wednesday with us, make it official: stop by Makeover on Main and get your residence card.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Two minutes, free, and everything you collect starts counting.

speaker: The Heroine
text: So remember, LAiDIES: you'll need more than a cup of ambition to keep up in the male-dominated world of AI.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Lucky for you... this series comes in small sips.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Oh — and every episode ends with a "Remember, LAiDIES." If you've got a sharper one than mine — one that would make Dolly proud — post it in the rooms: our residents-only chats at the sorority house in SUNNYVAiLE.

text: ICQ walked so our chat rooms could run.

text: We're trailblazers here.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Not idea thieves.

text: See you next Wednesday... in SUNNYVAiLE.
